----------------------------------------------------------------
1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY
----------------------------------------------------------------
Method:  Staggered Difference-in-Differences (DiD) complemented by an event-study.

Why?
•  The policy is introduced at different times across regions → classic staggered treatment.  
•  We observe the same individuals (or at least the same regional cells) annually before and after adoption.  
•  The question is average causal impact on employment and wages → level-change, not discontinuity, so DiD is natural.  
•  An event-study around adoption lets us (i) test pre-trends and (ii) trace dynamic effects.

Estimator: Use modern staggered-DiD estimators that handle treatment-timing heterogeneity, e.g. Callaway & Sant’Anna (2021) or Sun & Abraham (2020), implemented in the did or fixest packages.



----------------------------------------------------------------
2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL
----------------------------------------------------------------
Unit of analysis: individual i in region r, year t.

Treatment indicator:  
T_ir t  = 1 if region r has implemented the new labor-market policy by year t and 0 otherwise.

Treatment timing: Let  τ_r  be the first year the policy is in force in region r.  Treated observations are those with t ≥ τ_r.

Control group / counterfactual:  
•  Never-treated regions during the entire sample, plus  
•  Not-yet-treated regions in years before their own adoption (“not-yet-treated” serve as controls until they adopt).  
The combination is needed by modern staggered estimators.

No RDD → no running variable.



----------------------------------------------------------------
3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS
----------------------------------------------------------------
A1.  Parallel trends (conditional on controls)
     In the absence of the policy, treated and control regions would have followed the same trend in employment and wages.  
     Plausibility: The policy is nation–wide legislation phased in exogenously by administrative capacity rather than local labor conditions (institutional notes). We can bolster plausibility with pre-trend tests and differential region-specific controls.

A2.  No anticipation
     Workers and firms do not alter behavior before formal implementation.  
     Plausibility: Roll-out dates were not publicly announced far in advance; we can test for “placebo leads.”

A3.  Stable unit treatment value (no spillovers)
     Outcomes in one region are unaffected by adoption elsewhere.  
     Plausibility: Some cross-border commuting may violate this, especially in neighboring metro areas; we’ll test robustness excluding border counties.

A4.  Composition stability
     The set of resident workers in each region is stable or migration is exogenous to the policy.  
     Plausibility: Possible migration response; we will examine mobility patterns and re-weight to constant demographics.

A5.  Proper treatment-timing estimator
     The estimator must correctly aggregate treatment effects with heterogeneous timing (avoid two-way FE bias).  
     Plausibility: Using Callaway-Sant’Anna or Sun-Abraham satisfies this.



----------------------------------------------------------------
4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATION
----------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Endogenous adoption (regions adopt because of deteriorating labor markets).  
    •  Include rich pre-policy covariates and region fixed effects.  
    •  Event-study pre-trend test; drop regions failing parallel-trend tests.  
    •  Instrument roll-out timing with administrative capacity measures if available (robustness).

2.  Migration / composition changes.  
    •  Track cohort of individuals observed in consecutive years; use IPW to re-weight to baseline demographics.  
    •  Estimate effects on in-migration/out-migration separately.

3.  Contemporaneous region-specific shocks (e.g., plant closures).  
    •  Add region-specific linear trends or higher-order flexible trends.  
    •  Control for region-year covariates: industry mix, local GDP, unemployment insurance generosity, etc.  
    •  Conduct placebo test on an outcome that should not respond (e.g., hours of TV watched).



----------------------------------------------------------------
5. R CODE OUTLINE
----------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# --------------------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)            # fast fixed-effects & Sun-Abraham
library(did)               # Callaway & Sant’Anna
library(modelsummary)      # nice tables

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load data
# --------------------------------------------------------------
df <- read_csv("labor_survey_1980_1995.csv")

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable construction
# --------------------------------------------------------------
df <- df %>%
  mutate(
    post          = if_else(year >= policy_year_region, 1, 0),  # 1 after adoption
    treat         = if_else(!is.na(policy_year_region), 1, 0),  # ever-treated indicator
    rel_year      = year - policy_year_region,                  # event time
    employment    = as.numeric(employed == 1),
    ln_wage       = log(wage)                                   # winsorise beforehand if needed
  )

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 3A.  Sun & Abraham style TWFE with cohort-specific leads/lags
# --------------------------------------------------------------
event_spec <- feols(employment ~ sunab(policy_year_region, year) +
                                X(age + educ + gender + race) |
                                region + year,
                    data = df, cluster = ~region)
etable(event_spec, se = "cluster")

# 3B.  Callaway & Sant’Anna estimator
cs_est <- att_gt(yname   = "employment",
                 tname   = "year",
                 idname  = "id",
                 gname   = "policy_year_region",  # treatment cohort
                 xformla = ~ age + educ + gender + race,
                 data    = df,
                 clustervars = "region")
agg_effects <- aggte(cs_est, type = "dynamic")
summary(agg_effects)

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Main regression for log wages
# --------------------------------------------------------------
wage_spec <- feols(ln_wage ~ treat*post + X(age + educ + gender + race) |
                               region + year,
                   data = df %>% filter(year %in% 1980:1995),
                   cluster = ~region)
summary(wage_spec)

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness check: Drop border regions
# --------------------------------------------------------------
border_regions <- read_csv("border_regions.csv") %>% pull(region)
robust_spec <- update(wage_spec, data = df %>% filter(!region %in% border_regions))
summary(robust_spec)
```
Notes:  
•  `X()` inside fixest partials out controls.  
•  For the Sun-Abraham call we rely on fixest’s built-in ‘sunab’ operator.  
•  Cluster at the region level to allow serial correlation.



----------------------------------------------------------------
6. EXPECTED RESULTS
----------------------------------------------------------------
Economic theory predicts that easing labor-market regulation (if that is the policy) raises employment and may put modest downward pressure on wages; tightening regulation does the opposite. Assuming the policy made hiring easier:

•  Employment-to-population ratio: +2 to +4 percentage points within three years.  
•  Log wages: +0.5 % to +1.5 % (≈0.005–0.015 log points) for incumbents, possibly zero for entrants.



----------------------------------------------------------------
7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (DiD)
----------------------------------------------------------------
C1 Parallel pre-trends ……………………………………… 1  
C2 No anticipation of treatment ………………………… 1  
C3 No spillovers/SUTVA …………………………………… 0  
C4 Exogenous treatment timing ………………………… 0  
C5 Stable composition of units ………………………… 0  

(1 = satisfied/plausible; 0 = potentially problematic. Items C3–C5 will be probed via robustness and sensitivity analysis.)

----------------------------------------------------------------
